title: Final: hash tables and prefixes
sub: Recognize the technique from the statement, predict a trace, find a bug, explain out loud
cards/0/q: A playlist: song durations in seconds, up to 6·10⁴ songs. How many pairs of songs i < j have a total duration divisible by 60? Which technique?
cards/0/options/0: A remainder counter: for each song add count[(60 − t % 60) % 60], then count[t % 60]++
cards/0/options/1: Sort and walk with two pointers moving towards each other
cards/0/options/2: A “prefix → how many times” dictionary of prefix sums
cards/0/explain: This is pair counting from Two Sum, only on remainders: the partner of song t is a song with remainder (60 − t % 60) % 60. The outer % 60 is for t divisible by 60: their partner is remainder 0, not 60. There are 60 remainders — an int[60] is enough. Add first, then store, so a song does not find itself. O(n) time, O(1) memory.
cards/0/wrong/1: Converging pointers look for an exact sum in a sorted array. Here any sum divisible by 60 will do — 60, 120, 180…, and the pairs are scattered across the whole array.
cards/0/wrong/2: Prefixes are for contiguous segments. Here it is any pair of two songs, not a segment.
cards/1/q: A string of lowercase English letters. Can its letters be rearranged into a palindrome?
cards/1/options/0: int[26]: count the letters; at most one counter may be odd
cards/1/options/1: Sort it and compare with its reverse
cards/1/options/2: A HashSet of distinct letters: there must be at most half the length of them
cards/1/explain: In a palindrome letters stand in symmetric pairs — except perhaps one in the centre. That is a “how many times?” question → an int[26] counter, then a parity check. O(n) time, O(1) memory.
cards/1/wrong/1: A sorted string is not necessarily a palindrome: “aab” sorted is “aab”, reversed “baa”, yet these letters do make the palindrome “aba”.
cards/1/wrong/2: A set loses the quantities. “aabbc” makes the palindrome “abcba”, yet it has 3 distinct letters — more than half the length.
cards/2/q: New statements from games. Match the problem with the technique.
cards/2/pairs/0/0: Thousands of queries “total damage over frames l..r”
cards/2/pairs/0/1: An array of prefixes: P[r + 1] − P[l]
cards/2/pairs/1/0: The longest stretch of a match with equal wins and losses
cards/2/pairs/2/0: Can a word be built from the letters in the inventory
cards/2/pairs/2/1: int[26]: plus the inventory, minus the word
cards/2/pairs/3/0: Are there 5 consecutive values among the item ids
cards/2/pairs/3/1: HashSet, count from the start of a run
cards/2/pairs/4/0: The smallest free slot number with no extra memory
cards/2/pairs/4/1: Value v goes into slot v − 1
cards/3/task: A new problem: how many segments of [2, −2, 3, 0, −3, 1] sum to zero (k = 0). The rig stops once — predict how much count grows.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: x = −3: sum is 0 again, need = 0 − 0 = 0. By how much does count grow?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: Prefix 0 occurred twice — the empty one and the one after [2, −2] — so two new zero-sum segments end here: [2, −2, 3, 0, −3] and [3, 0, −3]. count = 2 + 2 = 4. +3 would come out if the current prefix were stored before the check: with k = 0 it would find itself.
cards/4/q: Product of Array Except Self. On [1, 2, 3, 4] this code returns [24, 24, 24, 24] instead of [24, 12, 8, 6]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/4/explain: ans[i] must get the product strictly left of i — prefix as it is. prefix * nums[i] includes the element itself: after the first pass ans = [1, 2, 6, 24], and every number ends up in its own product. The invariant: write first, then prefix *= nums[i].
cards/5/q: What is true about the complexity? Select all.
cards/5/options/0: Group Anagrams with a sorted-letters key is O(n·k log k), k being the word length
cards/5/options/1: First Missing Positive is O(n²): there is a while inside the for
cards/5/options/2: Longest Consecutive Sequence counting only from run starts is O(n)
cards/5/options/3: Subarray Sum Equals K with a prefix dictionary is O(n log n)
cards/5/options/4: A lookup by a string key of length k costs O(k): the hash is computed over every character
cards/5/explain: Sorting each word is k log k, and there are n words. In First Missing Positive every swap puts a number in place for good — at most n swaps, O(n) overall. In Longest Consecutive all the while loops together visit each number once. The prefix dictionary is one pass with O(1) on average per step, so O(n). And a string key is hashed in full on every lookup.
cards/6/q: A Unity project (C# 9, .NET Standard 2.1). How do you increment a counter in a Dictionary<int, int> for a key that may not exist yet?
cards/6/explain: GetValueOrDefault exists in .NET Standard 2.1 and returns 0 for a new key. That is two lookups, but in Unity it is the honest option. A single lookup via CollectionsMarshal is .NET 6+ only.
cards/6/wrong/1: CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault arrived in .NET 6; the .NET Standard 2.1 profile does not have it — it will not compile in Unity.
cards/6/wrong/2: For a new key counts[key] throws KeyNotFoundException, and for an existing one Add throws ArgumentException: the key is already there.
cards/7/q: A new problem: how many contiguous segments have a sum divisible by k (numbers can be negative). Put the steps of the out-loud explanation in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: is k > 0? can numbers be negative, what are n and the values
cards/7/items/1: Name the brute force over segments with a running sum — O(n²)
cards/7/items/2: Idea: a segment is divisible by k when two prefixes have the same remainder
cards/7/items/3: Structure: an int[k] remainder counter, starting with count[0] = 1 for the empty prefix
cards/7/items/4: Code: remainder ((sum % k) + k) % k, first add count[r], then count[r]++
cards/7/items/5: A run on a small example and the complexity: O(n) time, O(k) memory
cards/7/items/6: Edge cases: negative sums, k = 1, sum overflow
cards/7/explain: The same frame as Subarray Sum Equals K: a prefix, a partner by exact value, a counter that starts with the empty prefix. Only the key changes — a remainder, and with it a C# trap: % keeps the sign, hence the normalization.
cards/8/options/0: A prefix dictionary starts at {0: 1}, otherwise segments starting at index 0 are lost
cards/8/options/1: An int[26] can be a Dictionary key — anagrams will find each other
cards/8/options/2: Longest Consecutive Sequence iterates over the set, not the original array
cards/8/options/3: For the longest segment summing to k, the prefix index is overwritten on every occurrence
cards/8/options/4: A Span<int> from stackalloc cannot be stored in a class field
cards/8/explain: The empty prefix is the start for segments beginning at index 0. An array as a key is compared by reference: every word gets its own group, which is why the counter is turned into a string. Iterating over the set guarantees each run start is counted once. The longest segment needs the leftmost prefix index — write it on first occurrence and never overwrite. A Span lives only inside the method.
